title: Tim Berners-Lee & the Semantic Web
principle: Meaning should be machine-readable, so that independent parties can exchange it without agreeing on a schema first.

anchor.title: The Semantic Web
anchor.author: Tim Berners-Lee, James Hendler and Ora Lassila
anchor.note: The article that put the idea in front of a general audience. The wider programme — RDF, OWL, linked data, and later Solid — is in Block 7.

rows.pattern: Machine-readable meaning as the target — a graph a machine can act on rather than a document it can only parse
rows.where: The estate's graph substrate and the concept document that sets out its thinking

rows.pattern: Meaning attached to nodes (RDF's typed-resource model)
rows.where: **Deliberately inverted.** The estate derives meaning from edges instead, and the concept document states the inversion as a correction rather than a variation

rows.pattern: Meaning derived from connection between things
rows.where: The edge-first graph model the estate's ontology work is built on

rows.pattern: Personal data under the person's own control (Solid pods)
rows.where: Encrypted vaults, keyed by their holder — compared to pods explicitly, as complementary architectures with different threat models

rows.pattern: Interoperation with Solid itself — a vault that can read or write a pod
rows.where: Nowhere. The brief is an architectural comparison, not an integration
